core_principles: Maintain strict whole-body tension to keep the body aligned as a single rigid segment
Position the wrists directly below the shoulders so that the arms are perpendicular to the supporting surface in the static position
Minimize inter-segmental rotation at the elbow, shoulder, and hip during the flight phase of plyometric push-ups
common_mistakes: Pronounced hip flexion or segmental motion during the flight phase
specific_findings: A 5° shoulder-flexion perturbation during flight displaces the CoM from the nominal pendular arc by approximately L·cos (θ0)·δ ≈ 0.05 m for representative anthropometry (L = 0.60 m, θ0 = 12°)
At short flight times (tflight = 0.30 s, LOW = 0.50 m), the height discrepancy between models is ∆h = 0.020 m

core_principles: Ensure the arms are fully extended and oriented vertically (perpendicular to the floor) in the initial configuration.
Maintain a stable ankle joint to act as a fixed pivot, minimizing translational displacement of the ankle at takeoff during explosive push-ups.
Keep the body rigid to function as a single-segment pendulum rotating about the ankle pivot during the flight phase.
common_mistakes: Minor translational displacement of the ankle at takeoff.
Arms not perpendicular to the supporting surface in the initial setup.
specific_findings: Minor translational displacement of the ankle at takeoff is more common in recreational than in trained push-up execution.
For a body mass of 75 kg at VH, 0 <= 3.0 m/s, the peak aerodynamic drag force Fd is approximately 0.5 N.
For representative anthropometric values (LOW ≈ 0.7–0.9 m), the upper bound hand takeoff velocity is VH,0 <= 3.7–4.2 m/s.

core_principles: Maintain strict body tension throughout the movement, particularly during the flight phase of plyometric push-ups.
Keep whole-body alignment secure to prevent unwanted inter-segmental joint motion at the hips and shoulders.
common_mistakes: Failing to maintain strict body tension, leading to inter-segmental joint motion at the hip and shoulder during the flight phase.
Loss of whole-body alignment during the flight phase.
specific_findings: Reported ICC values of 0.80–0.96 for force-plate-derived flight time (t H).
For a uniform-rod body approximation, the compound-pendulum equivalent length ratio Leq/L is approximately 1.11–1.33.
The two-point mass model for CoM location introduces positional errors proportional to (1 – cosθ0).
Numerical agreement between quadrature and ODE implementations established a maximum discrepancy of < 2.5 × 10−7 s.
